summary: Burbank packs roughly 106,000 people into just 17 square miles wedged between the Verdugo Mountains and the flat floor of the San Fernando Valley — and yet it functions less like a bedroom suburb than like a small city with its own economic gravity, anchored by the Walt Disney Company and Warner Bros. Discovery headquarters, plus NBCUniversal's facilities spilling across its southern edge. That concentration of major entertainment employers means a median household income of nearly $153,000, unusually high for an L.A.-area city of this density, but the median home still costs over $1.1 million — a price-to-income ratio above seven — so buying requires either substantial savings or dual high incomes, while renting at $2,460 runs more manageably at roughly 19% of that median gross. The geography delivers a genuine split personality: south of the 134 freeway is flat, gridded, and walkable around a compact downtown with sit-down restaurants, independent coffee shops, and a well-attended farmers' market, while the hillside streets north toward the Verdugos offer canyon-mouth trail access and ridgeline sunset views toward the Pacific. With 9.7 hours of average daily sunshine and highs averaging 76°F, the climate leans warm and dry enough that summer heat in the valley basin becomes the real seasonal punctuation, not rain. Burbank is essentially a studio-lot company town that outgrew that label — prosperous and self-contained, but tethered to an industry whose fortunes will always shape what happens next.
